status_summary: As of 2026-10-07 administration of these programs is moving away from ED's day-to-day management, but their funding structure is unchanged and the administration's FY2027 request keeps Title I and IDEA as formula programs. Under interagency agreements announced on 2025-11-18, Labor takes a greater role in administering federal K-12 programs (K-12 Dive reports that Title I and other elementary and secondary programs are included; Labor's release does not name Title I, and the Mandate named HHS), and a 2026-06-16 agreement shifts day-to-day management of OSERS, which runs IDEA, to HHS; OSERS staff began moving into HHS space in early September 2026, while ED retains statutory responsibility and IDEA funds continue to flow through ED. The FY2027 budget document (April 2026) keeps Title I at $18.4 billion, raises IDEA State Grants by $489 million while folding in six smaller IDEA programs, and requests $2 billion for a Make Education Great Again grant that consolidates 17 other K-12 programs (the budget text describes it as a consolidation giving states more flexibility, which AASA calls a state block grant), so consolidation is proposed for other programs but not for Title I or IDEA, and the Education section proposes no transfers to HHS. No Title I phase-out, IDEA block grant or per-child account was found, and Congress funded ED in FY2026 and rejected the requested cut and program moves, per Federal News Network.

timeline.event: The Departments of Labor and Education announce interagency agreements (DOL release 25-1512-NAT): an Elementary and Secondary Education Partnership under which Labor takes a greater role in administering federal K-12 programs (managing competitions, providing technical assistance and folding programs into employment and training programs) and a Postsecondary Education Partnership for most Higher Education Act grant programs, both with oversight by the Education Department. The Labor release does not name Title I; K-12 Dive reports that Title I and other Office of Elementary and Secondary Education programs are assigned to Labor.

FY2026 appropriations for ED are enacted (Pub. L. 119-75, per a coalition letter of 2026-09-30). Federal News Network reports Congress rejected the requested $12 billion cut and the proposal to move core programs.

AASA summarizes the FY2027 request: Title I Part A level-funded at 18.4 billion dollars, IDEA increased, and a Make Education Great Again grant program consolidating 17 programs worth 6.5 billion dollars into a 2 billion dollar grant; neither Title I nor IDEA is described as block-granted or phased out. NAESP (2026-04-16) reports IDEA state grants of 15.4 billion dollars, a net increase of 522 million.

The President's FY2027 Budget (document posted under an April 2026 path; the date is that of AASA's summary) requests $76.5 billion in discretionary budget authority for the Department of Education (down $2.3 billion, 2.9 percent, from 2026); keeps Title I at $18.4 billion; raises IDEA State Grants by $489 million while folding six smaller IDEA programs into them (total IDEA about $16 billion); requests $2 billion for a new 'Make Education Great Again' (MEGA) grant consolidating 17 programs totaling $6.5 billion, eliminates 12 other programs totaling $2.1 billion, and sends Career and Technical Education to Labor. The Education section proposes no transfers to HHS and does not block grant Title I or IDEA; it describes MEGA as a consolidation that gives states more flexibility.

ED announces an agreement under which HHS takes over day-to-day management of OSERS and IDEA programs. ED keeps statutory responsibility and enforcement authority; funding continues through ED for now.

House Education and Workforce Committee Republicans release a ten-bill package; H.R. 9610 would transfer elementary and secondary programs, including Title I, to Labor. The reporting does not mention block grants, and it does not mention IDEA.
timeline.source: Daily Signal (posted by House Education and Workforce Committee)

timeline.event: Senate HELP Committee advances S. 5046 (13-9), led by Sen. Kaine with Sens. Collins and Murkowski, which would prohibit transfers of programs from four ED offices including OSERS and the elementary and secondary office. Committee Chairman Cassidy opposed the bill and opposes moving special education to HHS.

Government Executive reports ED began moving some employees into other agencies' buildings the previous week, with OSERS to HHS and the elementary and secondary office to Labor under 14 interagency agreements.
